lines: Lecture six. Genetic programming. Evolving programs themselves.
Normally, you write the program.
In genetic programming, you give examples of what it should do,
and evolution finds a program that matches.
A program can be drawn as a tree.
It runs from the leaves up to the root.
Change the input, and a different branch is used.
We build programs from two sets: functions, and terminals.
We grow downwards, picking parts at random.
At the depth limit, only terminals are allowed.
Run the program on many inputs.
The error is the area between its curve and the target.
Lower error means a fitter program.
Mutation: pick a node at random.
Cut off its subtree.
Grow a new random subtree in its place.
Crossover: pick a point in each parent.
Swap the two subtrees.
The same nodes, but the children have new sizes.
Here are four random programs. Lower error is better.
Next generation: a copy, a mutant, and two children.
A few generations later, we find x squared plus x plus one.
Five things to choose before a run.
Only plus and minus? You can only draw straight lines.
Add multiply, and the curve fits.
Remember: tell the computer what to do, not how.
A program is a tree, so we mutate and cross subtrees.
Fitness is the error on your examples.
